<reflection>
Excellent discrimination. The higher catalyst concentration clearly favors mechanisms with bimolecular catalyst interactions: M13, M19, M18, M2 are leading. M7 (substrate-catalyst bimolecular) also does well. Mechanisms without cat-cat interactions (M1, M10, M15, etc.) cluster together at ~-50. Top 4 candidates (M13, M19, M18, M2) all involve bimolecular catalyst behavior:
- M13: 2cat => inactive_cat2 (irreversible cat dimerization)
- M19: cat+catS => inactive_cat2S (mixed deactivation)
- M18: 2catS => inactive_cat2S2 (catS dimerization)
- M2: 2cat <=> cat2 (reversible dimerization, not deactivation)
</reflection>

<hypothesis>
To distinguish between M13, M19, M18, and M2, I should design an experiment that probes the time evolution of deactivation differently. 

Key distinction: M2 has REVERSIBLE dimerization (no permanent deactivation) while M13, M18, M19 are IRREVERSIBLE deactivation. A low catalyst/high substrate experiment with long time to full conversion would:
- Allow us to observe whether catalyst fully deactivates before full conversion (M13, M18, M19) or completes reaction (M2)
- M18 depends on [catS]^2, which is high when substrate is abundant (fast deactivation early)
- M19 depends on [cat][catS], also high when substrate abundant
- M13 depends on [cat]^2, deactivation mostly at start then levels off as cat→catS
- M7 (still in play): substrate-catalyst bimolecular productive pathway

Using high substrate with low catalyst creates a long reaction window and different [catS] profiles - M18/M19 should predict much slower later phases than M13.
</hypothesis>
